introduction.text: The Galleria Spada is a museum in Rome housed in the historic Palazzo Spada, notable for its Baroque architecture, forced perspective gallery, and collection of 16th‑17th‑century paintings.

history.description: The Palazzo Spada was originally built in 1540 for Cardinal Girolamo Capodiferro.
In 1632 Cardinal Spada purchased the palazzo and commissioned Francesco Borromini to redesign it, creating the famous forced perspective gallery.
The Galleria Spada was opened to the public in 1927 after the Italian State acquired the building.
The gallery closed during the 1940s and reopened in 1951 after restoration efforts.
The collection largely derives from the private holdings of Bernardino Spada, supplemented by works from Virgilio Spada.

design.description: Francesco Borromini’s forced perspective gallery features diminishing columns and a rising floor, creating the illusion of a 37‑meter long corridor that is actually only 8 meters.
The palazzo’s façade and interior stuccowork were crafted by Bartolomeo Baronino and Giulio Mazzoni, exemplifying Baroque ornamentation.
The Room of the Popes contains fifty inscriptions on the walls describing the lives of selected pontiffs, commissioned by Cardinal Bernardino Spada.

art.description: Portrait of Cardinal Bernardino Spada (1631) by Guido Reni, a key example of Baroque portraiture.
Portrait of Cardinal Bernardino Spada (1631) by Guercino, showcasing dramatic chiaroscuro.
The Revolt of Masaniello by Michelangelo Cerquozzi, a dynamic Baroque painting.
Saint Cecilia by Artemisia Gentileschi, illustrating the artist’s powerful depiction of music.
David with the Head of Goliath by Orazio Gentileschi, a dramatic biblical scene.
Christ and the Samaritan by Giovanni Battista Gaulli, a Baroque religious work.
